previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old female was admitted with worsening bilateral leg and hand swelling, shortness of breath, and mild erythema in the right leg, five days after completing IV antibiotics for recurrent cellulitis. She had gained 5 pounds recently and reported decreased urine output with foamy urine. Workup revealed no deep vein thrombosis, normal cardiac enzymes, and a suboptimal echocardiogram showing grossly normal systolic function. Her INR was subtherapeutic at 1.8, so she was bridged with enoxaparin. Due to mild signs of cellulitis, she was started on oral clindamycin. Her dyspnea was attributed to possible obstructive lung disease given her 60-pack-year smoking history, and she was discharged with albuterol and ipratropium inhalers. Lisinopril was reduced to 10 mg daily due to reported hypotension. She improved clinically and was discharged home with follow-up for INR monitoring, stress testing, and pulmonary function tests.

There is no pneumatosis or free air.  Visualized osseous structures are
unremarkable.

ULTRASOUND-GUIDED LONG DUAL-LUMEN VENOUS ACCESS LINE PLACEMENT

HISTORY:  ___ female with morbid obesity and inability to lie supine,
requires dual-lumen intravenous access for medication for colonoscopy and for
heparin infusion.

MEDICATION:  The patient received 3 cc of 1% buffered lidocaine over the left
cephalic vein access point in the distal arm.

PROCEDURE NOTE IN DETAIL:  Informed consent was obtained from the patient
outlining the risks and benefits of the proposed procedure.  The patient was
then brought to the Angiography Suite.  Given the patient's inability to lie
prone, it was not possible to position the patient on the angiography table
and perform fluoroscopy.  
Scars from previous upper arm venous cutdown for challenging venous access
were noted. A decision was made to perform ultrasound only guided venous
access with the patient sitting upright in a stretcher.  

The arm was extended on ___ stand.  The left upper extremity was prepped
and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A pre-procedure timeout was
performed.  Under ultrasound guidance a diminutive but patent left cephalic
vein was identified and accessed under real time ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture needle. Ultrasound images of the target vein were saved to PACS
before and after establishing venous access. A 0.018 wire was easily advanced
approximately 20 cm; however, some resistance was felt at this point. Given
the inability to perform fluoroscopy, it was not apparent whether this
represented a venous stenosis or other reason for non-advancement. Given the
patient's IV requirements a decision was made to place a 20 cm long line.  A 2
mm incision was made along the access needle and a 5 ___ peel-away sheath
advanced.  The dual-lumen 5 ___ PICC line was then cut to 20 cm and
advanced over the wire.  The peel-away sheath was removed.  Blood return was
obtained from both lumens and the catheter flushed normally.  
To clarify the position the patient was moved briefly towards the image
intensifier and an image of the left side of the chest and axillary fossa was
obtained.  Contrast was injected to the PICC line confirmed position within
the distal cephalic vein at the level of the axillary vein inflow.  Catheter
was secured and sterile dressings were applied.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated placement of a 5 ___ dual-lumen long line
measuring 20 cm.  The line was placed via the left cephalic vein and
positioned at the level of the cephalic vein/axillary confluence.  Although
not central, the catheter may be used immediately for infusion therapy.  
Given the venographic findings, this access could be used to place a PICC line
centrally if required in the short or medium term.

HISTORY:  ___ woman continues for recurrent cellulitis with lower
abdominal discomfort, assess for obstruction or extraluminal air.  

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph ___.  

FINDINGS:

Three frontal views of the abdomen show a normal bowel gas pattern.  There is
distention of the transverse colon which is normal on supine view.  There is
no pneumatosis or free air. There are degenerative changes in the included
spine.  

IMPRESSION:

No dilated loops of small bowel to suggest obstruction or ileus.

HISTORY:  Lower abdominal discomfort, please evaluate left lower pannus for
drainable fluid collection.

TECHNIQUE:  Limited ultrasound of the anterior abdominal wall.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:

Targeted sonographic imaging was performed in the region of discomfort
indicated by the patient, in the left anterior abdomen.  Imaging of the
patient's pannus at this location shows no evidence of focal fluid collection
to suggest abscess.  The echogenic line seen on some images corresponds to a
skin fold.  

IMPRESSION:

No abscess in the left anterior abdominal wall at the site of discomfort.
